stories.title: PNG parliament to consider Bougainville region's bid for independence
stories.summary: Papua New Guinea's autonomous region of Bougainville moved a step closer to possible independence on Thursday as the country's parliament prepared to consider the results of a non-binding referendum in which voters overwhelmingly backed secession. Residents of Bougainville, which consists of two main islands and several smaller ones with a population of about 370,000 people, voted 97.7% in favour of independence in 2019. But it has taken years of negotiations between the national and regional governments to get to the next step. Papua New Guinea's parliament must ratify the referendum result for it to take effect, and the two sides agreed this month that parliament would begin considering it on Thursday. No date for a vote has been announced. Leaders on Bougainville, which has had an independence movement for decades, have targeted greater self-government in September 2027 and full sovereignty in 2030. Bougainville's push for independence stems largely from longstanding grievances over control of revenue from the now-closed Panguna copper and gold mine and a decade-long civil war that killed thousands.

stories.title: The question dominating Indian politics: Is it worse when women swear?
stories.summary: Recent footage of young women swearing during a protest in India has sparked an unusual debate: are expletives worse when they come from women? The latest to weigh in has been opposition MP Rahul Gandhi who criticised Prime Minister Narendra Modi's description of seeing young women swearing as a "culture shock". "If boys swear, there is no problem and it is allowed. But if a girl swears, it is a cultural shock," Gandhi said. The protesters had been directing their anger at the government and some of the foul language targeted the prime minister, leading to outrage among his supporters, with even many critics of Modi's politics saying the women had crossed a line. The protests ended a month ago, but Rahul Gandhi's remarks have renewed the debate over how female activism, women voicing their views, stridently - even with expletives - are viewed in the country. It started last month when some young women used foul language against the prime minister during the weeks-long Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protests in Delhi and other cities, seeking education reforms. Modi himself addressed the issue in a selfie video where he said it was "a culture shock" to see young women using expletives, but added that he forgave them. The prime minister, however, did not comment on the violent police crackdown against the protesters or support women who said they had been trolled and had received rape threats for attending the CJP protests. At the weekend, Rahul Gandhi, who serves as the leader of the opposition in the lower house of the Indian parliament, criticised Modi's "culture shock" comment at a gathering of students in the western city of Pune. Pointing out that both male and female protesters had used foul language during the protest over exam paper leaks, he asked why was Modi only talking about women? His comments came weeks after posters and videos of female protesters insulting Modi went viral on social media.
